title: Individual Taxation - Adjustments to Income (Above-the-Line Deductions)
exam_relevance: HEAVILY TESTED - Expect 4-6 questions on CPA REG exam about adjustments to income, particularly IRA contributions, self-employment tax deduction, student loan interest, and HSA contributions. Understanding AGI is critical.
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between adjustments (above-the-line) and deductions (below-the-line)
Know why AGI is important (threshold for many tax calculations)
Master IRA contribution rules (traditional vs Roth, deductibility, limits, phase-outs)
Understand self-employment tax deduction (50% of SE tax)
Know student loan interest deduction (limits and phase-outs)
Understand HSA contribution rules and limits
Calculate AGI given gross income and various adjustments

introduction.why_important: Adjustments to income (above-the-line deductions) are subtracted from gross income to arrive at Adjusted Gross Income (AGI). AGI is critical because it's used as a threshold for many tax calculations, including itemized deduction limitations, credit phase-outs, and tax on social security benefits.
introduction.calculation_flow: Gross Income - Adjustments = AGI - Deductions (Standard or Itemized) = Taxable Income
introduction.exam_importance: Know which deductions are adjustments (above-the-line) vs itemized (below-the-line). Adjustments are better because they reduce AGI and don't require itemizing.
introduction.advantage_of_adjustments: Available to ALL taxpayers regardless of whether they itemize. Itemized deductions only benefit if total exceeds standard deduction.

why_agi_is_important.agi_definition: Adjusted Gross Income = Gross Income - Adjustments to Income

agi_used_as_threshold_for.medical_expense_floor: Medical expenses deductible only to extent > 7.5% of AGI
agi_used_as_threshold_for.casualty_loss_floor: Casualty losses subject to 10% of AGI floor (for federally declared disasters)
agi_used_as_threshold_for.charitable_contribution_limits: Cash contributions limited to 60% of AGI, appreciated property to 30% of AGI
agi_used_as_threshold_for.credit_phase_outs: Many credits phase out based on AGI (EITC, child tax credit, education credits)
agi_used_as_threshold_for.ira_deduction_phase_outs: Traditional IRA deduction phases out based on AGI (if covered by retirement plan)
agi_used_as_threshold_for.roth_ira_contribution_phase_outs: Roth IRA contributions phase out based on AGI
agi_used_as_threshold_for.social_security_taxation: Amount of SS benefits taxable depends on AGI + tax-exempt interest + 50% of benefits
agi_used_as_threshold_for.passive_loss_25000_exception: Real estate rental loss exception phases out starting at AGI $100,000

why_agi_is_important.exam_emphasis: Lower AGI is better - reduces floors/limits and increases eligibility for credits and deductions

moving_expenses.exception_military: ACTIVE DUTY military members can still deduct moving expenses for permanent change of station

deductible_part_of_self_employment_tax.rule: Can deduct 50% (one-half) of self-employment tax as adjustment to income
deductible_part_of_self_employment_tax.rationale: Employers deduct their share of employment taxes; self-employed should get similar benefit

calculation.step_1: Calculate SE tax = 92.35% of net self-employment income × 15.3% (or tiered rates)
calculation.step_2: Deduction = 50% of SE tax calculated in step 1
calculation.important: This deduction does NOT reduce SE tax itself (already factored in). It reduces income tax.

deductible_part_of_self_employment_tax.exam_emphasis: Deduct 50% (one-half) of SE tax. This is adjustment to income, NOT reduction of SE tax.

types.sep_ira: Simplified Employee Pension - employer contributions only
types.simple_ira: Savings Incentive Match Plan - for small employers with ≤100 employees
types.solo_401k: Individual 401(k) - for self-employed with no employees

sep_ira.contribution_limit: Lesser of: (1) 25% of net self-employment income (after SE tax deduction), or (2) $66,000 (2023) / $69,000 (2024)
sep_ira.deductible: Contributions deductible as adjustment to income

simple_ira_2024.employer_contribution: Either: (1) 3% matching, or (2) 2% nonelective for all eligible employees
simple_ira_2024.deductible: Employee deferrals deductible as adjustment; employer contributions deductible as business expense

self_employed_sep_simple_qualified_plans.exam_note: Self-employed retirement plan contributions are adjustments to income

self_employed_health_insurance.who_qualifies: Self-employed individual (sole proprietor, partner, >2% S corporation shareholder)

deduction.amount: 100% of health insurance premiums for self, spouse, dependents, and children under age 27
deduction.includes: Medical, dental, long-term care insurance (subject to age-based limits for LTC)

self_employed_health_insurance.where_deducted: ADJUSTMENT to income (above-the-line), not business expense on Schedule C
self_employed_health_insurance.exam_emphasis: 100% deductible as adjustment (not on Schedule C). Limited to SE income. Cannot take if eligible for employer plan.

traditional_ira.contributions: MAY be deductible (depends on AGI and retirement plan coverage)

roth_ira.distributions: TAX-FREE if qualified (account ≥5 years and age 59½, disabled, first home $10K, or death)

spouse_covered_not_you_mfj.rationale: More generous phase-out if you're not covered but spouse is

calculating_agi.formula: Gross Income - Adjustments to Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI)

adjustments.sep_ira_contribution: $80,000 - $5,652 = $74,348 × 25% = $18,587 (but limited to $66,000 max, so use calculated amount)

problem_1.question:
Taxpayer, age 35 and single, has the following for 2024:
- Salary: $60,000
- Covered by employer 401(k) plan
- Contributed $7,000 to traditional IRA
- AGI before IRA deduction: $60,000

What is the deductible IRA contribution?

A) $0
B) $3,500
C) $6,500
D) $7,000
problem_1.explanation:
The full $7,000 contribution is deductible. 

Analysis:
- Contribution limit: $7,000 (age under 50)
- Covered by retirement plan: Yes (401(k))
- AGI: $60,000
- Phase-out range for single covered by plan (2024): $77,000 - $87,000

Since AGI ($60,000) is BELOW the phase-out range ($77,000), the FULL contribution is deductible.

A is wrong - full deduction available below phase-out.
B and C are wrong - no phase-out applies at this income level.
problem_1.exam_tip: Traditional IRA: If covered by retirement plan, deduction phases out. Single phase-out (2024): $77K-$87K. Below $77K = fully deductible.

problem_2.question:
Self-employed taxpayer has net self-employment income of $100,000. Self-employment tax is $14,130. What is the deduction for self-employment tax?

A) $7,065
B) $14,130
C) $15,300
D) $0
problem_2.explanation:
The deduction for SE tax is 50% (one-half) of the SE tax paid.

Calculation:
SE tax = $14,130 (given)
Deduction = $14,130 × 50% = $7,065

This $7,065 is an ADJUSTMENT to income (reduces income tax, not SE tax).

B is wrong - cannot deduct full SE tax, only 50%.
C is wrong - this would be 15.3% of gross income (SE tax rate), not the deduction.
D is wrong - SE tax is partially deductible.
problem_2.exam_tip: SE tax deduction = 50% of SE tax. This is adjustment to income, doesn't reduce SE tax itself.

problem_3.question:
Taxpayer paid $3,500 in student loan interest during 2024. Taxpayer is single with AGI of $70,000. What is the student loan interest deduction?

A) $0
B) $2,500
C) $3,000
D) $3,500
problem_3.explanation:
The student loan interest deduction is limited to a MAXIMUM of $2,500, even though taxpayer paid $3,500.

Analysis:
- Interest paid: $3,500
- Maximum deduction: $2,500
- AGI: $70,000
- Phase-out range (single, 2024): $80,000 - $95,000

Since AGI ($70,000) is below the phase-out range, the full maximum deduction of $2,500 is allowed.

A is wrong - deduction is available (below phase-out).
C is wrong - no $3,000 limit; maximum is $2,500.
D is wrong - maximum is $2,500, not unlimited.
problem_3.exam_tip: Student loan interest: Maximum $2,500 deduction. Phases out at higher incomes ($80K-$95K single in 2024).

problem_4.question:
Taxpayer divorced in 2017. Under the divorce decree, taxpayer pays $20,000 per year in alimony and $10,000 per year in child support. What is the deduction for payments in 2024?

A) $0
B) $10,000
C) $20,000
D) $30,000
problem_4.explanation:
For PRE-2019 divorces (this divorce was in 2017), alimony is DEDUCTIBLE to payor and child support is NOT deductible.

Breakdown:
- Alimony: $20,000 - DEDUCTIBLE (pre-2019 divorce rules apply to all years)
- Child support: $10,000 - NOT deductible (never deductible)

Total deduction = $20,000

Note: The divorce occurred in 2017, so pre-2019 rules apply for all years, including 2024.

A is wrong - alimony under pre-2019 rules is deductible.
B is wrong - this is child support amount (not deductible); alimony is deductible.
D is wrong - child support is not deductible.
problem_4.exam_tip: Pre-2019 divorce = alimony deductible. Post-2018 divorce = alimony NOT deductible. Child support NEVER deductible. Know the cutoff date (12/31/2018).

problem_5.question:
Taxpayer, a self-employed consultant, has net self-employment income of $50,000 and paid $6,000 for health insurance for herself and her family. She is not eligible for any employer-sponsored health plan. What is the deduction for health insurance?

A) $0 - must be claimed as itemized deduction
B) $3,000 - limited to 50% of SE income
C) $6,000 - fully deductible as adjustment
D) $6,000 - deductible on Schedule C
problem_5.explanation:
Self-employed health insurance is 100% deductible as an ADJUSTMENT to income (above-the-line), subject to limitation.

Analysis:
- Health insurance premiums: $6,000
- Net SE income: $50,000
- Limitation: Deduction cannot exceed SE income
- Eligible for employer plan: No

Since $6,000 < $50,000 and taxpayer is not eligible for employer plan, the FULL $6,000 is deductible as an adjustment to income.

A is wrong - this is adjustment to income, not itemized deduction.
B is wrong - no 50% limitation; 100% deductible up to SE income.
D is wrong - deducted as adjustment (Form 1040), NOT on Schedule C business expenses.
problem_5.exam_tip: Self-employed health insurance: 100% deductible as adjustment (not on Schedule C). Limited to SE income. Cannot take if eligible for employer plan.

tip_1_above_vs_below_the_line.below_the_line: Itemized deductions or standard deduction - subtracted from AGI to get taxable income
tip_1_above_vs_below_the_line.why_adjustments_better: Reduce AGI (which affects many thresholds). Available to all taxpayers (don't need to itemize).
tip_1_above_vs_below_the_line.exam_approach: Know which deductions are adjustments vs itemized

tip_3_ira_deduction_rules.roth_not_deductible: Roth IRA contributions never deductible (but qualified distributions tax-free)

tip_4_se_tax_deduction.rule: Deduct 50% (one-half) of SE tax as adjustment to income

key_concepts: Adjustments (above-the-line) reduce gross income to arrive at AGI
AGI is critical threshold for many deductions, credits, and phase-outs
Adjustments are better than itemized deductions (reduce AGI, available to all)
Major adjustments: IRA, student loan interest, SE tax (50%), self-employed health insurance, HSA
IRA deduction phases out if covered by retirement plan (based on AGI and filing status)
Traditional IRA: may be deductible, distributions taxable. Roth IRA: not deductible, qualified distributions tax-free
SE tax deduction: 50% of SE tax, reduces income tax (not SE tax)
Self-employed health insurance: 100% deductible, limited to SE income, can't take if eligible for employer plan
Student loan interest: max $2,500, phases out at higher income
Alimony: pre-2019 divorces = deductible; post-2018 = NOT deductible. Child support never deductible.
HSA: triple tax benefit (deductible, tax-free growth, tax-free distributions for medical)
critical_for_exam: Know which deductions are adjustments vs itemized
IRA deductibility phase-outs: Single $77K-$87K, MFJ $123K-$143K (if covered by plan)
SE tax deduction: 50% of SE tax
Self-employed health insurance: 100%, limited to SE income
Student loan interest: max $2,500, phases out $80K-$95K (single)
Alimony cutoff date: 12/31/2018 (before = deductible, after = not)
common_mistakes: Thinking Roth IRA contributions are deductible (NO - never deductible)
Not applying IRA phase-out when covered by retirement plan
Thinking SE tax deduction reduces SE tax (NO - reduces income tax)
Deducting self-employed health insurance on Schedule C (NO - adjustment on 1040)
Not capping student loan interest at $2,500 maximum
Applying wrong alimony rules (pre-2019 vs post-2018)
Thinking child support is deductible (NO - never deductible)
Not recognizing HSA eligibility requirement (HDHP required)
